question: Why does the Beets lane reproduce badly (31.3% spread at n=3) while Fastify reproduces to 1.7%?

inputs.per_task_method: Codex reports cumulative thread totals; a task's cost is its final usage snapshot minus the previous task's.

finding: Beets does not vary because one task is unstable. Per-task variability is comparable in both lanes; what differs is whether it cancels. In Fastify the per-task deviations offset (cancellation ratio 12.4x) and no replicate is consistently dear. In Beets they align (ratio 1.1x): one replicate is the most expensive in 6 of 7 tasks and another the cheapest in 6 of 7, so deviations compound instead of averaging out.
mechanism: The workflow is one persistent session, so context accumulates across tasks and roughly two thirds of weighted cost is cached input. A session that pulls in more context early carries that penalty into every later task. Fastify re-converges -- its cheapest first task, r2 at 87,056 against 152,573, still ends with the largest final context -- so early exploration is traded against later exploration and final context lands within 5%. Beets never re-converges: final context spreads 40%.
not_supported: Cache warming across runs: the cached share of input is flat at 95.5-97.3% across all six sessions.
A single pathological task: the spread is distributed, with task-07 contributing 35%, task-05 21% and task-06 20%.
Task file overlap: both lanes change exactly one distinct production file per task.
consequence: At three replicates the Beets lane cannot resolve a treatment effect below roughly 30%. Fastify at 1.7% can resolve far smaller effects. Adding Beets replicates narrows the median but does not remove the compounding, because the correlation is within a session rather than between sessions. Selecting low-variance tasks is not a usable lever: Beets task-04 is quiet but is followed by tasks spreading 36%, 36% and 60%, and in a persistent session a later task inherits whatever divergence preceded it.

per_task_ranking.note: Beets task-04 is the lowest-variance task in either lane at 3.5%, so it is not true that every Beets task is unstable. Its low increment is partly offsetting rather than intrinsic: at that point the replicates' carried context differed 22.5% while their step counts differed 18.2% in the opposite direction (11, 11, 13), so the two nearly cancel within the task.

convergence.finding: Both lanes diverge immediately and only one recovers. Cumulative carried context is already 88.3% apart after Fastify task-01 and 44.4% apart after Beets task-01. Fastify then closes: 31.6%, 16.3%, 7.8%, 6.6%, 4.9% by the final task. Beets does not: 28.8%, 31.4%, 22.5%, 28.6%, 32.8%, 39.6%. The distinguishing property is convergence of accumulated context, not per-task stability.

rebuild_test.change: Beets rebuilt from 7 independent beetsplug modules to 6 tasks in the beets/ core package (2026-08-20).
rebuild_test.prediction_registered_before_r1: If front-loading is what makes a lane converge, the rebuilt lane should still reproduce badly, near 31.3% rather than Fastify's 1.7%.
rebuild_test.conclusion: Sharing a code region is not the lever. The rebuilt lane is materially cheaper -- 573,627 and 713,166 against 862,731 to 977,781 for the plugin set -- but no less variable, and it front-loads less than the set it replaced. Task selection therefore does not explain the difference between the lanes. Fastify's convergence remains unexplained and is the thing to investigate; the remaining candidates are the persistent-session design itself, the intrinsic open-endedness of the Beets tasks, and repository or language differences that the two-lane contrast cannot separate.
rebuild_test.cost_note: A cheaper lane that is equally noisy is not progress: resolving a treatment effect depends on spread, not on the total.
